title: The Merchant's Mysterious Last Will (ZH)
summary: A dying merchant leaves three sealed jars of dirt, bones, and straw to his three sons. Birbal decodes the profound fatherly inheritance.
full_text:
A wealthy merchant of Delhi died, leaving behind an enormous fortune and three sons. However, when his will was opened before the family elders, they found no mention of gold or property. Instead, the will instructed that three sealed ceramic jars be delivered to his sons:

To the eldest son: a jar filled with dry dirt and soil.

To the second son: a jar filled with dry animal bones.

To the youngest son: a jar filled with dry yellow straw.

The sons were insulted and bewildered. 'Our father was a millionaire, yet he has left us dirt, bones, and straw! Has our father gone mad?'

The brothers began fighting violently over their father's gold, palaces, and cattle, each claiming the entire estate. The bitter dispute was brought before Emperor Akbar.

Akbar examined the jars in confusion: 'Birbal, what father leaves dirt and bones to his children?'

Birbal smiled with deep admiration for the deceased merchant:

'Sire, this father was a man of supreme wisdom. He did not leave insults; he left a complete, fair division of his estate in symbolic code!

'To the eldest son, he gave the jar of dirt—which represents his vast real estate, farmland, orchards, and ancestral soil! Let the eldest son inherit all the lands!

'To the second son, he gave the jar of bones—which represents the cattle, horses, sheep, and livestock that possess skeletons! Let the second son inherit all the herds and animals!

'To the youngest son, he gave the jar of straw—which represents the golden harvest, the grain warehouses, the cotton stores, and the gold mohurs earned from agricultural trade! Let the youngest son inherit the treasury and warehouses!'

The three brothers stared in stunned silence. The code was so brilliant, so harmonious, and so perfectly balanced that all three brothers embraced with tears of joy, praising their late father's memory.

Akbar rewarded Birbal with a necklace of emeralds, marvelling at how wisdom can translate apparent nonsense into profound harmony.
